author: Dan Passarelli
title: Option Contract: Right Without Obligation
body: An option gives the holder the right—but not the obligation—to buy (call) or sell (put) a fixed quantity of an underlying asset at a specified strike price on or before expiration. Standard equity contracts represent 100 shares. For every long contract there is a corresponding short contract—they are equally common.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Open Interest vs. Volume
body: Volume = contracts traded in a day. Open interest = contracts currently open. New buyer + new seller → OI increases by 1. Existing holder closes with existing short → OI decreases by 1. Volume can exceed OI if contracts are opened and closed multiple times in one day.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Option Moneyness: ITM, ATM, OTM
body: For calls: ITM = stock > strike; ATM = stock ≈ strike; OTM = stock < strike. For puts the relationship reverses: ITM = stock < strike; OTM = stock > strike. Intrinsic value exists only for ITM options. All premium above intrinsic value is time value (extrinsic value).

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Long Call Payoff: Hockey-Stick Shape
body: Every long call at expiration has a hockey-stick payoff: flat at −premium (max loss) below the strike, then a 45-degree rising line above the strike. Break-even = strike + premium paid. Maximum loss is the premium; upside is theoretically unlimited.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Naked Call: Unlimited Risk, Limited Reward
body: Short naked call = limited premium collected, theoretically unlimited loss if stock rises. Profits only if stock stays below the strike at expiration. A covered call (long stock + short call) eliminates the unlimited-risk component because stock gains offset short-call losses above the strike.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Covered Call: Capped Upside, Reduced Cost Basis
body: Covered call = long stock + short call. Short call caps upside at the strike but reduces cost basis by the premium collected. If stock rises above the strike, shares get called away. Break-even = stock purchase price − premium received.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Short Put: Obligation to Buy at Strike
body: Selling a put creates an obligation to buy shares at the strike price if assigned. Break-even = strike − premium. Max profit = premium collected; max loss = strike − premium (effectively owning stock above market). Short puts are bullish and equivalent to covered calls via put-call parity.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Protective Put: Portfolio Insurance
body: Long stock + long put = a floor on downside. The put limits losses to (stock purchase price − strike + premium paid). Cost = put premium, analogous to insurance. Useful when bullish long-term but concerned about near-term volatility.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Black-Scholes Model: Six Inputs
body: BSM prices European calls using six inputs: stock price, strike price, time to expiration, risk-free interest rate, dividends, and volatility. Only volatility is not directly observable—it must be estimated (historical vol) or backed out from market prices (implied vol). This is the foundation of all option pricing.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Delta: Four Equivalent Definitions
body: (1) Rate of change of option value per $1 move in underlying; (2) slope of option price vs. underlying graph; (3) equivalent underlying shares per contract (delta × 100 for equity options); (4) approximate probability of expiring ITM (trader's heuristic, not exact). Call deltas: 0 to +1. Put deltas: −1 to 0.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Delta as ITM Probability Approximation
body: Delta ≈ probability of expiring ITM (simplified, not mathematically exact). 0.50 delta ATM call ≈ 50% chance ITM at expiry. 0.20 delta OTM call ≈ 20% chance. Useful heuristic for quick risk assessment, but ignores the distinction between risk-neutral and real-world probability.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Delta Behavior Across Strikes, Vol, and Time
body: ATM options: delta ≈ 0.50. Deep ITM → delta approaches 1.00. Deep OTM → approaches 0. Higher volatility pushes OTM deltas higher and ITM deltas lower. More time to expiration also raises OTM deltas. At expiration delta is binary: 0 or 1.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Gamma: Rate of Delta Change
body: Gamma = rate of change of delta per $1 move in underlying. Highest for ATM options near expiration; lowest for deep ITM/OTM. Long options have positive gamma (helpful convexity). Short options have negative gamma. Gamma causes large moves to benefit option buyers more than initial delta suggests.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Theta: Daily Time Decay
body: Theta = change in option value per unit of time. Long options: negative theta (lose value daily). Short options: positive theta (gain value daily). ATM options have the highest absolute theta. Theta accelerates as expiration approaches; it is not linear but steepens in the final weeks.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Higher Volatility Means Higher Theta
body: Higher vol = higher option prices = more time value = higher daily dollar decay. A $2 option decays faster in dollar terms than a $0.50 option. This is the flip side of gamma-theta: high vol = high gamma AND high theta. The leverage you pay for comes at a daily cost.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Vega: Sensitivity to Implied Volatility
body: Vega = change in option value per 1 percentage-point change in IV. Long options: positive vega (benefit from rising IV). Short options: negative vega. ATM options have the highest vega; deep ITM/OTM have less. LEAPS have much higher vega than short-dated options.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Put-Call Parity: The Foundational Equation
body: c + PV(strike) = p + S. Every call and put with the same strike and expiration are mathematically linked. Mispricing of one creates a riskless arbitrage. Rearranged: call = put + stock − strike + interest − dividends. This is the basis for all synthetic positions.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Rho: Interest Rate Sensitivity
body: Rho = change in option value per 1 percentage-point change in the risk-free rate. Calls: positive rho. Puts: negative rho. Negligible for short-dated options; significant for LEAPS (2-year call rho ≈ 0.858). Usually the least important greek for short-term traders.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Rho Scales With Time to Expiration
body: 22-day call rho ≈ 0.015. 2-year LEAPS rho ≈ 0.858. Rho increases with time because interest accrues over a longer period. In rising-rate environments, LEAPS traders must account for rho as a meaningful P/L factor.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Historical Volatility: Annualized Standard Deviation of Returns
body: HV = annualized standard deviation of close-to-close log returns. Convention: 252 trading days/year. Backward-looking—describes how volatile the stock has actually been. Does not directly predict future volatility. Used as a benchmark to compare against IV.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Implied Volatility: Forward-Looking Market Consensus
body: IV = the volatility input that makes a pricing model match the observed market option price. It is the market's collective forecast of future realized volatility. $100 stock at 32% IV implies ~68% probability the stock stays between $68–$132 over one year.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: IV Drivers: Fear, Greed, Events, and Arbitrage
body: IV rises from fear (protection demand), anticipated events (earnings, Fed), or speculative demand. IV falls from complacency, post-event vol crush, or market-maker arb. 'Buy the rumor, sell the news' manifests in IV rising into events and collapsing after.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: One-Day Standard Deviation from IV
body: Formula: IV / √(trading days/year) = 1-day expected σ. For $100 stock at 32% IV: 32 / 16 = 2%. ~68% chance of <$2 daily move. Useful for setting daily-move expectations and for gamma-scalping breakeven calculations.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: IV Mean Reversion: The Foundation of Vol Selling
body: IV oscillates around a characteristic range for each underlying. When IV deviates significantly above the mean → vol-selling opportunity. When depressed below the mean → vol-buying opportunity. Mean reversion is the foundation of most short-vol strategies.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: VIX: 30-Day Expected S&P 500 Volatility
body: VIX = CBOE's implied vol of a hypothetical 30-day SPX option. Represents the market's expectation of annualized S&P 500 vol over the next 30 days. VIX of 20 implies ~1.25% expected daily moves. The 'fear index'—spikes during crises, fades during calm. Mean-reverts strongly.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: IV Term Structure: Contango vs. Backwardation
body: Normal: longer-dated options have higher IV (contango). Pre-event: front-month IV spikes above back-months (backwardation). Understanding term structure identifies which expiration month is cheapest/richest on a volatility basis—critical for calendar spread strategy selection.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Volatility Skew in Equities
body: Equity skew: OTM puts trade at higher IV than ATM; ATM higher than OTM calls. Reflects demand for crash protection and fear. OTM puts can trade 10+ vol points above equidistant OTM calls. Known as a 'smirk' rather than a symmetric smile. Skew creates exploitable pricing discrepancies.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Risk Priority for Long Option Buyers
body: Priority: (1) delta = directional exposure, primary concern; (2) theta = time decay working against you; (3) vega = IV risk; (4) gamma = helpful on strong moves. Being correct on direction is not enough—theta and vega can cause losses if timing is off.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: ATM Options Have Peak Gamma
body: ATM options near expiration have the highest gamma—delta changes fastest per $1 move. Maximum leverage in the final weeks. For buyers: ATM gives maximum gamma sensitivity. For sellers: short ATM near expiration is the most gamma-dangerous position.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: ITM vs. ATM vs. OTM: Greek Comparison Table
body: ITM call (32.5 strike, $35 stock): delta=0.862, gamma=0.079, theta=0.010, vega=0.026—acts most like stock. ATM (35): delta=0.570, gamma=0.166, theta=0.013, vega=0.048—balanced. OTM (37.5): delta=0.185, gamma=0.119, theta=0.007, vega=0.032—most leveraged relative to premium, lowest win rate.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: OTM Call Buyers: Starting in the Hole
body: OTM calls have a high probability (~75–85%) of expiring worthless. Expected value can still be positive if the stock makes a large move, but buyers must be compensated by large wins to overcome frequent small losses. Buy OTM options only with strong conviction and a clear edge.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Options Leverage: Double-Edged Amplification
body: Small underlying moves can produce triple-digit % returns—or complete premium loss. One equity contract = 100 shares of exposure for the premium cost. Leverage cuts both ways. Options can also cap losses when used as hedges.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Options Are Fairly Priced: Edge Comes From Forecasting
body: Options are not systematically overpriced or underpriced in aggregate. Neither always-buy nor always-sell strategies have inherent edge. Edge comes from correctly forecasting vol, direction, or timing relative to what the market has priced in.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Gamma-Theta Tradeoff: The Core of Vol Selling
body: Vol-selling strategies profit from theta (positive daily decay) but suffer from gamma (losses from stock movement). These forces are inseparable: more theta income = more gamma risk. This is the fundamental tension in every short-volatility position.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Naked Call Setup: Sell Near Resistance in a Range
body: Sell a call when you believe the stock will stay below the strike at expiration. Best near the top of a trading channel/resistance. Greeks: negative delta (bearish-neutral), positive theta (daily income), negative gamma (risk from upside), negative vega (profits if IV falls). Max profit = premium collected.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Gamma Amplifies Losses Faster Than Delta Predicts
body: Short call with delta=0.34, gamma=0.15: if stock rises $1, new delta = 0.49. A stop-loss at 1.10 (on a 0.66 credit) is reached at only a $1.01 stock rise—not the $1.32 a pure-delta calculation implies. Gamma acceleration means stop-losses are hit faster than expected.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: More Theta Means More Gamma Near Expiration
body: As expiration approaches with stock near the strike: theta rises (more daily reward) AND gamma rises (more directional risk). They are inextricably linked. The best theta-collecting period is also the most gamma-dangerous period.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Whipsaw Risk: Higher Vol Causes False Stop-Outs
body: In volatile markets, stop-loss prices can be reached due to random noise rather than real directional moves. Trader exits for a loss; market reverses; trade would have recovered. Higher IV → wider effective stops needed to avoid whipsaw, but wider stops = larger potential losses.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Comparing IV Across Expiration Months for Short-Vol Entry
body: When selling vol, compare IV across months. March at 19.2% IV vs. April/May at 23%: March is cheapest by IV, offering less premium but possibly better risk-adjusted value. Higher-IV months reflect more uncertainty—decide whether the extra premium compensates for the added risk.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Put-Call Parity Enables All Synthetic Positions
body: Rearranging put-call parity: long call = long put + long stock; long put = long call + short stock. Any option position can be replicated with the other option type + stock. This equivalence enables synthetics, conversions, reversals, and arbitrage.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Synthetic Long Call = Long Put + Long Stock
body: Equivalent to buying a call per put-call parity. Used when the actual call is overpriced, unavailable, or has worse bid-ask spreads. The put + stock combination delivers the same payoff at expiration.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Synthetic Long Stock = Long Call + Short Put
body: Long call + short put (same strike, same expiration). At expiration: call exercised or put assigned = buy at strike either way. Forward price = strike + interest − dividends. Used by professionals to replicate stock exposure without tying up full capital.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Conversion and Reversal: Near-Riskless Arbitrage
body: Conversion = long stock + long put + short call (same strike/expiry). Net delta ≈ 0. Reversal = short stock + short put + long call. P/L = put-call parity discrepancy. Used by market makers to lock in mispricings between options and their synthetic equivalents.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Pin Risk: Assignment Uncertainty at Expiration
body: When stock price is very close to a strike at expiration, market makers cannot know if the option will be assigned. They face ±100 delta uncertainty. If they hedge incorrectly, they end up with an unintended stock position. Short option positions near ATM at expiration must be managed carefully.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Box Spread: Fixed-Value Arbitrage Instrument
body: Box = bull call spread + bear put spread (same strikes, same expiration). Value at expiration = upper strike − lower strike (always). Present value = (upper − lower) − interest. If the box trades below fair value, buying it locks in a riskless interest-rate return.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Interest Rates: Higher Rates Lift Calls, Depress Puts
body: From put-call parity: higher rates increase carrying cost → raise the forward price → raise call values → lower put values. Calls benefit when rates rise; puts are hurt. Rho makes this effect explicit in the pricing model.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: LEAPS in Rising Rate Environments
body: LEAPS calls have rho ≈ 0.8+. A 1% rate increase boosts their value by $0.80+. In rising-rate cycles, long LEAPS calls receive an additional tailwind. Long LEAPS puts face a headwind. LEAPS rho risk is significant enough to include in scenario analysis.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Dividends Lower Calls, Raise Puts
body: From put-call parity: call = put + stock − strike + interest − dividends. Higher dividends reduce call prices and increase put prices. Stock price drops on ex-date by ~the dividend amount, hurting calls and helping puts. Must enter accurate dividend forecasts into pricing models.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Four Dividend Dates: Ex-Date Is What Matters for Options
body: (1) Declaration date—amount and dates announced; (2) Ex-dividend date—stock trades without the dividend right; (3) Record date—registered shareholders receive dividend; (4) Payable date—dividend is paid. Options traders focus on the ex-date: the stock drops by ~the dividend amount here.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Deep ITM Calls May Be Exercised Early Before Ex-Date
body: If the time value of a deep ITM call < dividend amount, it is economically rational to exercise early to capture the dividend. This reduces call prices just before ex-dates. Short deep-ITM calls heading into ex-dates face early assignment risk.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Irregular Dividends Create Option Pricing Risk
body: Companies may cut, raise, or eliminate dividends unexpectedly. Using historical dividend estimates when the actual dividend has changed causes systematic mispricing. Always check declared (not estimated) dividend amounts before pricing options on high-dividend stocks.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Dividend Surprise: Impact on Long Calls
body: If XYZ raises its quarterly dividend from $0.10 to $0.40 unexpectedly, the stock price drops $0.30 more than expected on ex-date. A long ITM call valued at $1.65 using the 'wrong' dividend becomes $1.35 using the 'right' dividend—a $0.30 loss from incorrect dividend input alone.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Vertical Spread: Same Type, Same Expiry, Different Strikes
body: Buy and sell options of the same type (both calls or both puts), same underlying, same expiration, different strikes. Defines both maximum profit and maximum loss. Reduces cost and vega/gamma exposure vs. outright options. The foundation of most retail spread strategies.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Bull Call Spread: AAPL 395-405 Example
body: Buy AAPL Feb 395 call @ 14.60, sell Feb 405 call @ 10.20. Net debit: $4.40. Max profit: $5.60 (width − debit). Max loss: $4.40. Break-even: $399.40. Saves $10.20 vs. buying the outright call; sacrifices unlimited profit above $405.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Vertical Spread Crushes Vega and Gamma
body: AAPL 395 call alone: gamma=0.0097, vega=0.513. AAPL 395-405 spread: gamma=0.0001, vega=0.020. The spread reduces vega by 96% and gamma by 99%. Use spreads when directional conviction is high but you want minimal vol/time risk.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Correct Direction + Poor Timing = Losing Long Call
body: A trader can be right on direction and still lose money on a long call if theta erodes the premium before the move. Vertical spreads have much lower theta, making timing less critical. Trade-off: spreads also reduce sensitivity to large moves.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Bear Put Spread: Defined-Risk Bearish Trade
body: Buy higher-strike put, sell lower-strike put. Profits if stock falls to or below the short strike. Max profit at or below the short strike; max loss above the long strike. Lower cost and lower vega than outright puts. Best for modest bearish moves.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Credit vs. Debit Spreads Are Economically Equivalent
body: Bull call spread (debit) and bull put spread (credit) with the same strikes have identical at-expiration payoff profiles. The difference is premium flow direction and margin treatment. Choose based on bid-ask spreads, margin, and liquidity—not based on credit vs. debit preference.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Box Spread = Bull Call Spread + Bear Put Spread
body: A box = bull call spread + bear put spread (same strikes, same expiration) = fixed-value instrument worth exactly (upper − lower) strike at expiration. Professionals use boxes to lock in interest rates or arbitrage mispriced combinations of spreads.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Condor: Four-Strike Range Trade
body: Short condor: sell inner vertical spread, buy outer vertical spread for protection. Net credit. Maximum profit if stock stays inside the inner strikes at expiration. The width between inner and outer strikes defines the max-loss zone.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Iron Condor: Short OTM Put Spread + Short OTM Call Spread
body: Net credit received up front. Maximum profit if stock stays between the two short strikes at expiration. Defined max loss at the outer strikes. Combines a short put spread (below market) and a short call spread (above market). Lower capital requirement than a naked straddle.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Iron Butterfly: Sell ATM Straddle + Buy OTM Strangle
body: Short ATM call + short ATM put (straddle) + long OTM put + long OTM call (strangle). Maximum profit at the ATM strike at expiration. Capital-efficient vs. standard butterfly because OTM options often have tighter bid-ask spreads than ITM options.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Iron Condor Strike Selection: 1 Standard Deviation Rule
body: With QQQ at $55.95, 31 DTE, IV=23.2%, 35 trading days: 1σ ≈ $4.05. Short strikes at ±1σ: sell 55 put and 57 call; buy 54 put and 58 call for protection. Net credit: $0.63. Places short strikes at the boundary of the 'expected range' at expiration.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Iron Condor: Define Exit Rules for the Losing Leg Before Entry
body: When one leg is threatened by a directional move: options are close the spread, close only the threatened side, or roll to a further strike. No automatic action is always correct—requires judgment on continued directional risk. Define your max loss threshold before entering the trade.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Calendar Spread: Buy Back Month, Sell Front Month
body: Same strike, different expirations. Short front-month option decays faster than the long back-month (theta differential). Also a vega play: long calendar benefits from rising back-month IV relative to front-month. Maximum profit at expiration if stock is exactly at the short strike.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Calendar Spread P/L: Tent-Shaped at Near-Month Expiry
body: At near-month expiration: profit is highest if stock is at the short strike; losses accumulate if stock moves far away in either direction. After near-month expiration, trader owns the back-month option at a reduced cost basis = (original spread debit − time value captured).

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Rolling Calendars: Systematically Reducing LEAPS Cost Basis
body: Sell front-month calls against a LEAPS call each month. After 3 months collecting 1.50/month against a 4.00 LEAPS, aggregate credit = 4.50 > original cost—the long option is essentially 'free.' Risk: stock must stay near the short strike each month.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Term Structure IV Trade: Buying the Calendar
body: July IV at 45%, September IV at 38%. Buy the calendar (sell July, buy September) at 7-point IV differential. If July IV converges to September's 38%, profit ≈ $1,283 on a 210-lot equivalent. Risk: IVs diverge further, or stock moves away from strike causing the spread to collapse.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Selling Calendars: Unique Risk When Front Is Cheaper
body: If front-month IV is 17% and back-month IV is 25%, selling the calendar (buy front, sell back) seems attractive. But selling time spreads when back-month is elevated carries its own risk: if the back-month IV rises further, the short back-month hurts more than the long front-month helps.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Double Calendar: Both-Sided Theta + Vega Collection
body: Double calendar = long call calendar + long put calendar at different strikes, bracketing the current price. Benefits from stock staying in a range (theta) while having more strike options than a single calendar. Also a vol play: buying the double calendar profits from rising IV (long vega).

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Diagonal Spread: Calendar With Strike Offset
body: Buy far-month option at one strike + sell near-month at a different strike. Combines calendar characteristics (time spread, long vega) with vertical spread characteristics (directional delta). Bullish diagonal: buy lower-strike back-month, sell higher-strike front-month for income.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Delta-Neutral Trading: Isolate Volatility Exposure
body: Neutralize directional exposure by hedging delta with the underlying. The position then profits or loses primarily from changes in IV (vega) and/or magnitude of realized moves (gamma/theta)—not from direction. Requires continuous rebalancing as delta drifts.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Long Gamma Strategy: Profit From Realized Volatility
body: Long options + short delta hedge. Profits if realized vol > implied vol priced into the options. Each stock move enables a profitable hedge rebalance (gamma scalp). Risk: if stock moves less than expected, theta erodes the premium. Breakeven requires enough realized movement to cover total theta paid.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Delta-Neutral Mindset: Trade Vol, Not Direction
body: Ask: 'Is IV too high or too low vs. likely realized vol?' not 'Is the stock going up or down?' Buy when IV < expected realized. Sell when IV > expected realized. Hedge delta continuously to strip out directional noise and express a pure volatility view.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Establishing Delta Neutrality: The Stock Hedge Calculation
body: To neutralize a 20-lot long call position at 50 delta/contract (= 1,000 total long deltas): sell 1,000 shares. If resulting net delta is still slightly positive (+20), buy 20 more shares. Read greeks in a pricing model; adjust stock position to achieve near-zero net delta.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: P/L Attribution: Vega + Gamma + Theta Decomposition
body: Susie's IV trade: Vega P/L (+$3,000 from 3-point IV rise) − theta cost ($75) − delta/gamma loss ($225) = net $800 profit. Always decompose P/L into components. A net gain can mask a vega win offsetting a gamma loss. Attribution guides future sizing and diagnosis.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Vol Buying: Long Delta-Neutral Options Before Events
body: Buy delta-neutral options when IV is historically low, ahead of anticipated vol expansion. Profit from rising IV (vega) and/or gamma scalping on large moves. Risk: if no event materializes and IV stays low, theta erodes the position.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Volatility Buying vs. Selling: Same Underlying, Opposite Views
body: Bobby Buyer's approach (ch.12): buys delta-neutral options before an earnings event expecting a vol crush after a big move. Susie Seller's approach: sells delta-neutral options expecting the IV crush to profit more than any gamma scalps cost. Same stock, same setup, opposite vol views.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Gamma Scalping: Trading Realized Volatility
body: Long gamma trader sells stock when price rises (locks in positive delta gain), buys stock when price falls (re-neutralizes). Each rebalance captures a realized-move profit. Net P/L = sum of all stock scalps − total theta paid. Profitable if realized vol > implied vol.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Gamma Scalp Mechanics: Buy Dips, Sell Rallies
body: Long 20 ATM calls + short 1,000 shares. Stock falls $2: delta goes negative via gamma. Trader buys shares to re-neutralize (buys the dip). Stock rallies $3: delta goes positive. Trader sells shares (sells the rally). Each buy-low/sell-high cycle funds the theta cost.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Gamma-Theta Breakeven: Realized vs. Implied Vol
body: For gamma scalping to be profitable, the stock's realized daily moves must exceed what was priced into the options. Breakeven daily move ≈ option's implied 1-day σ. If realized vol > implied: scalps exceed theta. If realized < implied: theta destroys more value than scalps recover.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Short Gamma Forces Buying High, Selling Low
body: Short calls + long stock delta hedge: when stock rises, delta goes negative—must buy stock at rising prices. When stock falls, must sell at falling prices. Short gamma systematically forces buy-high/sell-low trades. Theta income compensates for this structural disadvantage.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Volatility Charts: Reading IV and Realized Vol Together
body: Plot IV and 30-day realized vol on the same chart over time. Key questions: (1) Is IV above/below its historical range? (2) Is IV above/below current realized vol? (3) Are they converging or diverging? This is the primary tool for identifying vol-selling and vol-buying setups.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Vol Pattern 1: Both IV and Realized Rise
body: Options are expensive in absolute terms but may reflect legitimate fear. If realized rises faster than IV: market underestimates actual moves—buy vol. If IV rises faster than realized: options are overpriced—vol-selling opportunity, but caution: realized may still catch up.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Vol Pattern 3: Realized Rises, IV Falls (Post-Earnings Crush)
body: Stock becomes more volatile, yet options become cheaper. Classic post-earnings: direction surprises but vol collapses after the announcement. Long gamma position before earnings benefits from realized outpacing IV. Short vol here would be painful.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Vol Pattern 7: Realized Falls, IV Rises (Pre-Earnings IV Rush)
body: The classic pre-earnings setup: stock is quiet but options become increasingly expensive as an event approaches. Options buyers profit if the eventual move exceeds IV expectations. Passarelli: 'the picture of the classic IV rush that is often seen in stocks around earnings time.'

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Vol Pattern 6: Realized Constant, IV Falls (Classic Short-Vol Setup)
body: IV falls while realized vol stays stable = vol premium is compressing. IV has been elevated and begins reverting to match realized, creating a profitable short-vol window. Two IV-to-realized convergences on one chart signal multiple entry opportunities.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Vol Pattern 9: Both IV and Realized Fall (Post-Crisis Normalization)
body: Both declining simultaneously = slow dissipation of a crisis period. Stocks stabilize, fear ebbs, options become cheaper. Short-vol strategies become attractive again after a period of elevated vol. Often coincides with market bottoms and post-event stabilization.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Long Straddle: Buy ATM Call + ATM Put
body: Profits from large moves in either direction. Break-even = strike ± total premium. Example: 70-strike straddle at $4.25/side = $8.50 total; break-evens at $65.75 and $74.25. Primary risk: IV collapse and/or realized moves too small to cover theta. The ultimate pure volatility long.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Straddle Vega: Maximum IV Sensitivity Per Dollar Spent
body: ATM straddle has the highest vega per dollar. Both call and put vega ≈ 0.05: total ≈ 0.10 per lot. 10-point IV rise = $100/lot gain. Long straddles are primarily vega plays in calm markets—they profit from IV expansion regardless of direction.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: When to Buy a Straddle: IV Below Historical Range
body: Buy straddles when IV is depressed below its historical range AND below recent realized vol. Goal: profit from IV normalizing upward (vega) or from large realized moves via gamma scalping. Key: enter early in a low-IV trend, not after IV has already started rising.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Short Straddle: Sell ATM Call + ATM Put
body: Maximum profit = total premium if stock is exactly at strike at expiration. Unlimited losses in both directions. Passarelli: 'one of the riskiest positions one can trade.' Only appropriate when IV is highly elevated and you're confident the stock will move less than the market expects.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Short Straddle: Define Max Loss Before Entry
body: Negative gamma compounds losses rapidly as the underlying moves. Critical discipline: define your max loss threshold before entry (e.g., close if position reaches 1.5× credit collected). Never average into a losing short straddle. The unlimited risk profile requires pre-defined exit rules.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Long Strangle: OTM Call + OTM Put
body: Lower cost than a straddle; requires a larger stock move to profit (break-evens farther from current price). Lower vega per dollar spent. Use when expecting a large move but wanting to reduce premium at risk. Trade-off: wider break-evens in exchange for less upfront cost.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Short Strangle: More Room for Error Than Short Straddle
body: Sell OTM call + OTM put. More premium than vertical spreads but unlimited risk. Key advantage: wider strikes provide wiggle room—stock can move moderately without losing. Best in high-IV environments when the stock is expected to stay within the short strikes.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Ratio Spread: Unequal Number of Options
body: Buy fewer options, sell more at a different strike (e.g., 1×2 call ratio). Net credit or lower cost. Extra short creates potentially unlimited risk beyond the short strikes. Can start delta-neutral but carries significant gamma risk as the underlying moves.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Backspread: Long More Options Than Short
body: Sell fewer options at one strike, buy more at a further strike (e.g., 1×2: sell 1 call, buy 2 calls at higher strike). Benefits from large directional moves AND rising IV. Used as a hedge against big moves or as a pure volatility-buying structure.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Backspread Greeks Flip With Stock Movement
body: A call backspread starts with positive gamma and positive vega. If the stock falls far below the short strike, vega and gamma turn negative—the position transforms from 'long vol' to 'short vol.' Understand the full risk profile across all price scenarios before entering.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Ratio Vertical Spread: Sell More Than Buy for Credit
body: Buy 1 call (or put) at a closer strike, sell 2 at a further strike. Creates a net credit or low debit but unlimited risk above the short strikes. Requires good prediction of both direction AND a limited range. Generally best avoided unless there is a specific edge in both vol and direction.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Market Maker Portfolio Management: Net Greek View
body: Market makers accumulate positions across many strikes/expirations by providing liquidity. They manage the combined net greek profile—not individual trades. Key skills: lower bids when long gamma/vega (don't want more); raise bids when short gamma/vega (need to hedge).

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Skew Trading: Sell Expensive Puts, Buy Cheap Calls
body: Equity vol skew makes OTM puts trade 4+ vol points above equidistant OTM calls. Risk reversal (sell OTM put, buy OTM call) profits if skew normalizes, regardless of stock direction. Can be delta-hedged to isolate the pure skew trade.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Delta Lean: Intentional Directional Bias in a Neutral Strategy
body: A delta lean means intentionally accepting some directional delta instead of staying perfectly neutral—usually when the trader has a mild directional view. Passarelli: a lean 'should be entered into a model for simulation before executing' to study the up/down risk. If it reduces overall position risk, it's justified.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Greeks Are a Complete Trading Framework
body: Greeks help at every stage: find trades (identify vol mispricing), plan execution (size positions), manage positions (monitor risk evolution), and plan exits (identify when the thesis is invalidated). Without greek literacy, option trading is guesswork.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Vol-Buying Setup: Rising Intraday Vol, Flat Close-to-Close HV
body: If intraday (high-low) vol increases significantly but close-to-close HV hasn't risen, the market may be underpricing actual activity. Buy delta-neutral options while maintaining slight directional bias. Divergences between different HV measures can signal mispriced IV.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Always Plan for Worst-Case Before Entering a Trade
body: Passarelli: 'You can plan for [unexpected moves]. And as an option trader, you have to.' Define max acceptable loss, exit triggers, and worst-case scenarios before entry. Options with defined max loss enforce this discipline. Unplanned losses are inexcusable.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: Would I Do It Now? Rule: Eliminate Sunk Cost Thinking
body: At any point while holding a position, ask: 'If I didn't have this position, would I enter it now at current prices?' If the answer is no, close it. This cuts through sunk-cost rationalization, hope-based holding, and cognitive bias. It forces honest reassessment of whether the original thesis still holds.

author: Dan Passarelli
title: The Greeks Are the Option Trader's Primary Resource
body: From finding trades, to planning execution, to managing and adjusting, to planning exits—greeks are the vocabulary and toolkit of professional option trading. They quantify risk, help identify edge, and allow customization of risk/reward to match any market forecast.
